screens.title: Integrating Red Hat Storage with OpenShift and OpenStack
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we bring together two enterprise storage solutions — Red Hat Ceph Storage and Red Hat Gluster Storage — and show how each integrates with OpenShift and OpenStack. You will learn why persistent storage matters for modern containerized applications, how OpenShift uses the Container Storage Interface to request volumes, and how OpenStack services like Cinder and Glance can use Ceph as a backend. I will point out concrete examples such as using Ceph RBD for a database volume, CephFS for shared file systems, and RGW for S3-compatible object storage. We will also cover the OpenShift Data Foundation operator pattern and common mistakes to avoid when configuring StorageClasses or Ceph clients. By the end of this chapter you will be able to map application requirements — shared file access, high-performance block, or object storage — to the appropriate Red Hat storage interface and plan safe, testable integrations. As you start, think about a stateful microservice you maintain and how its storage needs would be satisfied in these platforms.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Integrating Red Hat Storage
Integrating Red Hat Storage with OpenShift and OpenStack
Persistent volumes, StorageClasses and Ceph/Gluster backends for container and cloud platforms.
Why this matters
Stateful workloads require storage that survives pod lifecycle and delivers required performance and sharing semantics.
What you will do
Map application access modes to Ceph or Gluster, author StorageClasses and validate PVC lifecycle across OpenShift and OpenStack.
Explore Key Topics
Ceph RBD
High-performance block storage for databases and VM volumes.
CephFS & RGW
Shared POSIX file systems and S3-compatible object storage for apps and backups.
Gluster CSI
Shared file volumes via the Gluster CSI driver when that architecture fits.
Visual concept
OpenShift
Pod → PVC → StorageClass
CSI driver provisions an RBD, CephFS, or Gluster volume on demand.
OpenStack
Cinder/Glance → Ceph
Cinder provisions RBD volumes; Glance stores images as RBD, Nova uses RBD for disks.
Integration note
Use the OpenShift Data Foundation operator to deploy and manage Ceph for OpenShift. For OpenStack, configure service-specific cephx users with minimal permissions.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Across these screens you'll see four measurable objectives designed for architecture-level decisions. First, you will explain why persistent storage is necessary for stateful applications in container platforms, identifying how pods differ from VMs and why storage must outlive pod lifecycles. Second, you will configure Red Hat Ceph Storage as a persistent storage provider for OpenShift using the Container Storage Interface; that includes authoring a StorageClass and understanding the CSI secrets and parameters required for RBD and CephFS. Each objective pairs conceptual understanding with a concrete artifact you can inspect: YAML for a StorageClass or a PVC, and validation commands to confirm claims. Practice-oriented examples keep the focus on what you must validate in a real cluster, and each objective highlights a common misconception so you can avoid configuration traps. By the end of these two objective slides you will have a clear checklist for design and validation when planning production storage integrations.

screens.title: Why persistent storage matters in OpenShift
screens.narratorSegment: Containers are ephemeral by design: pods can be rescheduled, replaced, or scaled down without preserving local disk. Persistent storage exists to decouple application state from container lifetime. In practice that means using a PersistentVolume backed by an external system so your database files, caches, or user uploads survive pod restarts. A clear example is a PostgreSQL instance deployed in OpenShift. If you attach an RBD-backed PersistentVolume and the pod crashes, the data remains; a new pod can mount the same volume and recover. A common misconception is assuming ReadWriteOnce volumes allow multiple pods to write concurrently — for block storage that is usually single-writer. Contrast that with ReadWriteMany where CephFS or GlusterFS can be mounted by multiple replicas simultaneously. Another trap is assuming all storage has equal performance; block devices tuned for low latency are better for databases than network file systems. Finally, validate durability and backups: even when you use Ceph or Gluster, you must consider replication and backup strategies. Ask yourself: does my workload need single-writer high IOPS, or shared POSIX semantics? That decision drives which Red Hat storage interface you choose.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Persistent storage decouples application state from pod lifecycle; pick interfaces that match access and performance needs.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Why persistent storage matters
Definition
Persistent storage keeps state across pod lifecycle
Containers are transient. PersistentVolumes provided by Ceph or Gluster ensure your data is independent of pod scheduling decisions. Choose access modes and backend types to match workload requirements, and validate replication and backups.
Concrete example
A database uses Ceph RBD as a PersistentVolume. If the database pod is replaced, the RBD remains and can be reattached to the new pod preserving data integrity.
Misconception
Assuming ReadWriteOnce supports concurrent writers — for block devices it does not. Use CephFS or Gluster for ReadWriteMany semantics.
Key Takeaway

Pick the storage type to match access mode and performance needs; validate mounts and backups before production rollouts.

Analogy & scenario
Pet store vs. warehouse
Think of ephemeral containers as temporary cages. Persistent storage is a warehouse where goods are safely kept and can be retrieved regardless of the cage used. For databases, your warehouse must allow fast single-writer access; for shared configs, multiple cages may need simultaneous read/write access to the same shelves.
Check your understanding
If a web app requires all replicas to write log files to the same path, would RBD be sufficient? Why or why not?

screens.title: How CSI enables dynamic provisioning in OpenShift
screens.narratorSegment: The Container Storage Interface standardizes how Kubernetes-like orchestrators call out to external storage provisioners. In OpenShift, a developer creates a PersistentVolumeClaim which references a StorageClass. The StorageClass indicates a CSI provisioner and the parameters needed to create the real volume. The CSI controller receives the request and calls into the backend — Ceph or Gluster — to provision the RBD image or file volume and returns a PersistentVolume object to the control plane. The kubelet then uses the CSI node plugin to stage and mount the volume into the pod. A concrete walkthrough: a pod claims a StorageClass named ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd. The Ceph CSI provisioner creates an RBD image in the specified pool, stores metadata and secrets, and the pod mounts that device as a block device at runtime. A common mistake is misconfiguring CSI secrets namespaces or provisioner names so the controller cannot authenticate to Ceph. Always test a PVC lifecycle: create StorageClass, create PVC, bind, mount, write data, restart pod, and verify persistence. How would you detect whether the CSI provisioner created the RBD image successfully? Check the provisioner logs and Ceph pools for new images.

keyIdea.title: CSI lifecycle
keyIdea.text: PVC → StorageClass → CSI controller provisions backend volume → node plugin stages and mounts it for the pod.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › CSI provisioning flow
Overview
Dynamic provisioning with CSI
A StorageClass tells OpenShift which CSI driver to invoke and what parameters to pass to the storage backend.
Step 1
Developer creates a PVC referencing the StorageClass.
Step 2
CSI controller provisions a backend volume (RBD image or Gluster volume).
Step 3
Kubelet node plugin stages and mounts the volume into the pod.
Key Takeaway

CSI separates control plane provisioning from node-level mounting, enabling consistent dynamic provisioning across storage providers.

Annotated flow
PVC request
Claims storage with a named StorageClass.
CSI controller
Creates backend volume using provided parameters and secrets.
Node plugin
Stages and mounts the created device inside the pod.
Common mistake
Incorrect secret names or namespaces prevent the CSI provisioner from authenticating to Ceph; verify secret and provisioner parameters first.

screens.title: Ceph RBD StorageClass YAML example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's examine a real StorageClass example for Ceph RBD as used in OpenShift Data Foundation deployments. The StorageClass tells OpenShift to use the Ceph CSI provisioner openshift-storage. rbd. csi. ceph. com, identifies the clusterID and pool, and points to provisioner and node-stage secret names and namespaces. These secrets hold cephx credentials the CSI controller and node plugin use to talk to monitors and manipulate RBD images. Notice parameters like imageFeatures layering and allowVolumeExpansion true for online resizing. A common error is a typo in a secret key or referencing a secret in the wrong namespace; if so the provisioner will log authentication failures and the PVC will remain pending. Concrete example: after ODF deploys its operator it creates a storageclass named ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd. To validate, create a PVC using that StorageClass and check that oc get pvc shows a bound status and oc get pv lists an RBD-backed PV. If bound, confirm the RBD image exists in the Ceph pool and that the pod can write data and persist across restarts. This walkthrough teaches you to read StorageClass parameters and map them to Ceph concepts.

keyIdea.title: StorageClass anatomy
keyIdea.text: StorageClass parameters and secret references are critical for CSI to authenticate and provision RBD images correctly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Ceph RBD StorageClass
YAML example
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd
provisioner: openshift-storage.rbd.csi.ceph.com
parameters:
  clusterID: openshift-storage
  pool: ocs-storagecluster-cephblockpool
  imageFeatures: "layering"
  csi.storage.k8s.io/provisioner-secret-name: ocs-storagecluster-rbd-provisioner
  csi.storage.k8s.io/provisioner-secret-namespace: openshift-storage
  csi.storage.k8s.io/controller-expand-secret-name: ocs-storagecluster-rbd-provisioner
  csi.storage.k8s.io/controller-expand-secret-namespace: openshift-storage
  csi.storage.k8s.io/node-stage-secret-name: ocs-storagecluster-rbd-node
  csi.storage.k8s.io/node-stage-secret-namespace: openshift-storage
reclaimPolicy: Delete
volumeBindingMode: Immediate
allowVolumeExpansion: true
What to verify
Confirm secret names and namespaces exist, check operator-created pools, and ensure network access to Ceph monitors from control plane and nodes.
Explanation cards
clusterID & pool
Map StorageClass parameters to Ceph cluster identity and the block pool used for images.
CSI secrets
Controller and node secrets let CSI call Ceph APIs; they must contain cephx credentials with the right permissions.
allowVolumeExpansion
Allows resizing volumes without detaching; ensure underlying Ceph pool supports layering and expansion semantics.
Key Takeaway

Carefully map StorageClass parameters to Ceph pools and secrets, and test the PVC lifecycle to verify provisioning succeeds.

screens.title: Ceph storage types: RBD, CephFS, RGW
screens.narratorSegment: Ceph offers three complementary interfaces: RBD for block devices, CephFS for POSIX-compliant shared files, and RGW as an S3-compatible object gateway. Understand their tradeoffs to make correct design choices. RBD exposes block devices suitable for databases and VM disks; in OpenShift it is provisioned as a PersistentVolume that the pod mounts as a device. RBD is typically used with ReadWriteOnce semantics and prioritizes low latency and IOPS. CephFS exposes a distributed POSIX file system and supports ReadWriteMany, which makes it suitable for content management systems or shared configuration across replicas. RGW provides object endpoints for applications that use S3 APIs; it’s ideal for static assets, backups, or large unstructured data that benefit from object semantics. A common misconception is that object storage can replace POSIX semantics — it cannot; object APIs lack file locking and POSIX metadata. When designing an architecture, pick RBD for single-writer high-performance needs, CephFS for concurrent file access, and RGW for object APIs. Consider network topology and monitor reachability for all three, and test with representative workloads to validate latency and throughput assumptions. Ceph storage types: RBD, CephFS, RGW means rbd = block, cephfs = shared posix file system, rgw = s3-compatible object storage; pick based on access patterns.. In practical terms, choosing block, file, or object interfaces for workloads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Ceph storage types
Interface comparison
RBD (Block)
Single-writer, high performance
Best for databases and VM disks; exposes block devices as PVs.
CephFS (File)
POSIX shared filesystem
Allows multiple pods to mount the same filesystem concurrently.
RGW (Object)
S3-compatible object store
Used for backups, static assets, and applications using object APIs.
Decision checklist
  • Does workload need POSIX semantics? Use CephFS.
  • Does it need low-latency block I/O? Use RBD.
  • Does it use S3 APIs or store blobs? Use RGW.
Misconception

Object storage cannot provide POSIX semantics; do not try to use RGW where shared file locks and directories are required.

screens.title: OpenShift Data Foundation (ODF) operator
screens.narratorSegment: OpenShift Data Foundation, previously called OpenShift Container Storage, is the recommended operator-driven way to run Ceph for OpenShift workloads. The operator automates Ceph cluster deployment, pool creation, CSI driver deployment, and secret management so that storage can be consumed directly from the platform. Operationally, ODF can run the Ceph cluster within the OpenShift control plane or adjacent to it, depending on availability and resource planning. When you deploy ODF it creates StorageClasses, CSI provisioners, and the necessary cephx secrets in the openshift-storage namespace so that CSI controllers and node plugins can authenticate. A typical workflow is: deploy ODF operator, review created StorageClasses such as ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd, then create PVCs to validate. Be mindful of capacity planning: Ceph requires sufficient OSDs and appropriate replication settings for durability. A common operational mistake is treating the operator as a black box; you must still monitor Ceph health, OSD utilization, and network latencies between monitors and nodes. Design decision: colocate Ceph OSDs for low-latency with compute, or isolate them for dedicated storage clusters. Which approach suits your availability goals? OpenShift Data Foundation (ODF) operator means odf automates ceph lifecycle and csi setup for openshift, but architects must plan capacity, topology, and monitoring.. In practical terms, deploying and managing ceph inside or adjacent to openshift. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Operator benefits
keyIdea.text: ODF automates Ceph lifecycle and CSI setup for OpenShift, but architects must plan capacity, topology, and monitoring.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › OpenShift Data Foundation
Operator responsibilities
  • Deploy and configure Ceph monitors and OSDs
  • Create storage pools and manage CRs
  • Install CSI drivers and create StorageClasses
  • Provision cephx secrets and RBAC
Operational checklist
Capacity
Plan OSD count, replication, and erasure coding based on data durability targets.
Monitoring
Monitor Ceph health and network latency between monitors and compute nodes.
Topology
Decide whether to colocate OSDs with compute or isolate them in a dedicated storage tier.
Design note

Colocating OSDs reduces latency but increases resource contention. Isolate for predictable performance and easier scaling.

screens.title: Gluster StorageClass YAML example
screens.narratorSegment: Gluster integrates with OpenShift via a CSI driver that accepts a StorageClass indicating the Gluster provisioner and REST endpoint parameters. The StorageClass must include the REST URL, REST username, and secret details used to control volume provisioning on the Gluster cluster. After deploying the Gluster CSI driver and creating the StorageClass, a PVC referencing it will trigger dynamic Gluster volume creation. A concrete example StorageClass contains resturl pointing to the Gluster REST service and a secretName in the Gluster namespace. Validation steps: ensure the Gluster REST endpoint is reachable from OpenShift nodes, verify the secret contains correct admin credentials, and confirm the provisioner is registered in the cluster. A typical mistake is forgetting network routes or firewall rules between OpenShift nodes and the Gluster REST service; this leaves PVCs pending. Always test with a pod that mounts the volume using ReadWriteMany access to validate concurrent access patterns. This walkthrough helps you spot the fields the Gluster CSI expects and the runtime checks you should perform. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Ceph as the backend for OpenStack services
screens.narratorSegment: OpenStack uses Ceph as a highly integrated backend for multiple services. Cinder uses Ceph RBD to provide block volumes; when a user requests a new volume, Cinder provisions an RBD image from a designated 'volumes' pool. Glance can store VM images as RBD images in a separate 'images' pool, enabling efficient storage and thin provisioning. Nova can directly use RBD for ephemeral disks, which improves live migration by avoiding bulky image transfers. Manila can integrate CephFS to provide shared file systems to VMs. Ceph’s advantages for OpenStack include replication-driven durability, scalable object storage via RGW, and advanced features like snapshots and cloning that Cinder exposes to users. A common operational requirement is to configure separate cephx users for each OpenStack service — for example, cinder, glance, and nova — with least privilege permissions. Missteps here cause authentication failures or over-privileged principals. When you design the backend, choose pools and user mappings to align with performance and security zones, and validate by creating volumes, uploading images, and performing snapshots and clones to exercise the full lifecycle. screens.title: Ceph vs Gluster for OpenShift and OpenStack
screens.narratorSegment: Both Ceph and Gluster provide persistent storage for OpenShift, but they have different design points that influence your choice. Ceph is a unified platform offering block, file, and object storage with strong integration into OpenStack core services. Use Ceph when you need RBD for databases and VM volumes, CephFS for shared POSIX data, or RGW for S3-compatible object access. Gluster focuses on distributed file systems and can be a good fit when you want straightforward ReadWriteMany access and a simpler operational model for file-based workloads. A common architecture decision is to prefer Ceph when you need deep OpenStack integration or want a single storage platform covering multiple interfaces. Choose Gluster when the primary requirement is network file sharing and when the team is comfortable operating Gluster clusters. Misconceptions include thinking Gluster cannot be used with OpenStack — it can via Manila for shared file systems — or that Ceph always outperforms Gluster in every scenario. Performance depends on topology, hardware, and tuning. Validate using representative workloads: a database benchmark for RBD and concurrent file writes for Gluster or CephFS before committing to production.

screens.title: Common mistakes and validation steps
screens.narratorSegment: Integrations often fail for operational reasons rather than conceptual misunderstandings. Common mistakes include wrong StorageClass parameters or secret names, firewall or DNS issues between OpenShift nodes and Ceph monitors, misconfigured ceph. conf paths in OpenStack services, and over-privileged cephx users. To avoid these pitfalls, follow a short validation checklist: first, verify CSI pods are running and that StorageClasses exist; second, ensure secrets referenced by StorageClasses exist in the correct namespaces and contain valid cephx credentials; third, create a PVC and confirm it becomes bound; fourth, run a pod that mounts the volume and perform read/write tests, then restart the pod to confirm persistence. For OpenStack, create a Cinder volume and check that an RBD image is present in the Ceph pool, then test snapshot and clone operations. Automation and testing are your friends: include these checks in CI for platform changes. A misconception to watch is assuming a mounted volume implies correct replication or backup — always verify Ceph health and replication counts separately. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we bring together two enterprise storage solutions — Red Hat Ceph Storage and Red Hat Gluster Storage — and show how each integrates with OpenShift and OpenStack. You will learn why persistent storage matters for modern containerized applications, how OpenShift uses the Container Storage Interface to request volumes, and how OpenStack services like Cinder and Glance can use Ceph as a backend. I will point out concrete examples such as using Ceph RBD for a database volume, CephFS for shared file systems, and RGW for S3-compatible object storage. We will also cover the OpenShift Data Foundation operator pattern and common mistakes to avoid when configuring StorageClasses or Ceph clients. By the end of this chapter you will be able to map application requirements — shared file access, high-performance block, or object storage — to the appropriate Red Hat storage interface and plan safe, testable integrations. As you start, think about a stateful microservice you maintain and how its storage needs would be satisfied in these platforms.

Across these screens you'll see four measurable objectives designed for architecture-level decisions. First, you will explain why persistent storage is necessary for stateful applications in container platforms, identifying how pods differ from VMs and why storage must outlive pod lifecycles. Second, you will configure Red Hat Ceph Storage as a persistent storage provider for OpenShift using the Container Storage Interface; that includes authoring a StorageClass and understanding the CSI secrets and parameters required for RBD and CephFS. Each objective pairs conceptual understanding with a concrete artifact you can inspect: YAML for a StorageClass or a PVC, and validation commands to confirm claims. Practice-oriented examples keep the focus on what you must validate in a real cluster, and each objective highlights a common misconception so you can avoid configuration traps. By the end of these two objective slides you will have a clear checklist for design and validation when planning production storage integrations.

On this second objectives slide we focus on design and validation. You will understand the differences among Ceph RBD, CephFS, and Ceph RGW so you can choose the right interface: RBD for low-latency block volumes, CephFS for POSIX shared file systems, and RGW for object-accessed assets. You will also learn how to design storage solutions that leverage Ceph or Gluster across OpenShift and OpenStack, considering access modes, performance, and operator deployment models like the OpenShift Data Foundation. The objectives emphasize both authoring and testing: creating StorageClasses and PVCs, deploying an example pod to validate mounts or RBD attachments, and checking network connectivity and cephx authentication. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual mental model to help you remember when to pick each storage type, and a verification milestone to ensure you can demonstrate the capability in a lab or interview.

Containers are ephemeral by design: pods can be rescheduled, replaced, or scaled down without preserving local disk. Persistent storage exists to decouple application state from container lifetime. In practice that means using a PersistentVolume backed by an external system so your database files, caches, or user uploads survive pod restarts. A clear example is a PostgreSQL instance deployed in OpenShift. If you attach an RBD-backed PersistentVolume and the pod crashes, the data remains; a new pod can mount the same volume and recover. A common misconception is assuming ReadWriteOnce volumes allow multiple pods to write concurrently — for block storage that is usually single-writer. Contrast that with ReadWriteMany where CephFS or GlusterFS can be mounted by multiple replicas simultaneously. Another trap is assuming all storage has equal performance; block devices tuned for low latency are better for databases than network file systems. Finally, validate durability and backups: even when you use Ceph or Gluster, you must consider replication and backup strategies. Ask yourself: does my workload need single-writer high IOPS, or shared POSIX semantics? That decision drives which Red Hat storage interface you choose.

The Container Storage Interface standardizes how Kubernetes-like orchestrators call out to external storage provisioners. In OpenShift, a developer creates a PersistentVolumeClaim which references a StorageClass. The StorageClass indicates a CSI provisioner and the parameters needed to create the real volume. The CSI controller receives the request and calls into the backend — Ceph or Gluster — to provision the RBD image or file volume and returns a PersistentVolume object to the control plane. The kubelet then uses the CSI node plugin to stage and mount the volume into the pod. A concrete walkthrough: a pod claims a StorageClass named ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd. The Ceph CSI provisioner creates an RBD image in the specified pool, stores metadata and secrets, and the pod mounts that device as a block device at runtime. A common mistake is misconfiguring CSI secrets namespaces or provisioner names so the controller cannot authenticate to Ceph. Always test a PVC lifecycle: create StorageClass, create PVC, bind, mount, write data, restart pod, and verify persistence. How would you detect whether the CSI provisioner created the RBD image successfully? Check the provisioner logs and Ceph pools for new images.

Let's examine a real StorageClass example for Ceph RBD as used in OpenShift Data Foundation deployments. The StorageClass tells OpenShift to use the Ceph CSI provisioner openshift-storage. rbd. csi. ceph. com, identifies the clusterID and pool, and points to provisioner and node-stage secret names and namespaces. These secrets hold cephx credentials the CSI controller and node plugin use to talk to monitors and manipulate RBD images. Notice parameters like imageFeatures layering and allowVolumeExpansion true for online resizing. A common error is a typo in a secret key or referencing a secret in the wrong namespace; if so the provisioner will log authentication failures and the PVC will remain pending. Concrete example: after ODF deploys its operator it creates a storageclass named ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd. To validate, create a PVC using that StorageClass and check that oc get pvc shows a bound status and oc get pv lists an RBD-backed PV. If bound, confirm the RBD image exists in the Ceph pool and that the pod can write data and persist across restarts. This walkthrough teaches you to read StorageClass parameters and map them to Ceph concepts.

Ceph offers three complementary interfaces: RBD for block devices, CephFS for POSIX-compliant shared files, and RGW as an S3-compatible object gateway. Understand their tradeoffs to make correct design choices. RBD exposes block devices suitable for databases and VM disks; in OpenShift it is provisioned as a PersistentVolume that the pod mounts as a device. RBD is typically used with ReadWriteOnce semantics and prioritizes low latency and IOPS. CephFS exposes a distributed POSIX file system and supports ReadWriteMany, which makes it suitable for content management systems or shared configuration across replicas. RGW provides object endpoints for applications that use S3 APIs; it’s ideal for static assets, backups, or large unstructured data that benefit from object semantics. A common misconception is that object storage can replace POSIX semantics — it cannot; object APIs lack file locking and POSIX metadata. When designing an architecture, pick RBD for single-writer high-performance needs, CephFS for concurrent file access, and RGW for object APIs. Consider network topology and monitor reachability for all three, and test with representative workloads to validate latency and throughput assumptions. Ceph storage types: RBD, CephFS, RGW means rbd = block, cephfs = shared posix file system, rgw = s3-compatible object storage; pick based on access patterns.. In practical terms, choosing block, file, or object interfaces for workloads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

OpenShift Data Foundation, previously called OpenShift Container Storage, is the recommended operator-driven way to run Ceph for OpenShift workloads. The operator automates Ceph cluster deployment, pool creation, CSI driver deployment, and secret management so that storage can be consumed directly from the platform. Operationally, ODF can run the Ceph cluster within the OpenShift control plane or adjacent to it, depending on availability and resource planning. When you deploy ODF it creates StorageClasses, CSI provisioners, and the necessary cephx secrets in the openshift-storage namespace so that CSI controllers and node plugins can authenticate. A typical workflow is: deploy ODF operator, review created StorageClasses such as ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd, then create PVCs to validate. Be mindful of capacity planning: Ceph requires sufficient OSDs and appropriate replication settings for durability. A common operational mistake is treating the operator as a black box; you must still monitor Ceph health, OSD utilization, and network latencies between monitors and nodes. Design decision: colocate Ceph OSDs for low-latency with compute, or isolate them for dedicated storage clusters. Which approach suits your availability goals? OpenShift Data Foundation (ODF) operator means odf automates ceph lifecycle and csi setup for openshift, but architects must plan capacity, topology, and monitoring.. In practical terms, deploying and managing ceph inside or adjacent to openshift. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Gluster integrates with OpenShift via a CSI driver that accepts a StorageClass indicating the Gluster provisioner and REST endpoint parameters. The StorageClass must include the REST URL, REST username, and secret details used to control volume provisioning on the Gluster cluster. After deploying the Gluster CSI driver and creating the StorageClass, a PVC referencing it will trigger dynamic Gluster volume creation. A concrete example StorageClass contains resturl pointing to the Gluster REST service and a secretName in the Gluster namespace. Validation steps: ensure the Gluster REST endpoint is reachable from OpenShift nodes, verify the secret contains correct admin credentials, and confirm the provisioner is registered in the cluster. Both Ceph and Gluster provide persistent storage for OpenShift, but they have different design points that influence your choice. Ceph is a unified platform offering block, file, and object storage with strong integration into OpenStack core services. Use Ceph when you need RBD for databases and VM volumes, CephFS for shared POSIX data, or RGW for S3-compatible object access. Gluster focuses on distributed file systems and can be a good fit when you want straightforward ReadWriteMany access and a simpler operational model for file-based workloads. A common architecture decision is to prefer Ceph when you need deep OpenStack integration or want a single storage platform covering multiple interfaces. Choose Gluster when the primary requirement is network file sharing and when the team is comfortable operating Gluster clusters. Misconceptions include thinking Gluster cannot be used with OpenStack — it can via Manila for shared file systems — or that Ceph always outperforms Gluster in every scenario. Performance depends on topology, hardware, and tuning. Validate using representative workloads: a database benchmark for RBD and concurrent file writes for Gluster or CephFS before committing to production.
